subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN
subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a brief announcement to make concerning assistance to India under the Colombo plan. Out of the $50 million appropriated for Canada's participation in the Colombo plan
for the fiscal year 1960-61, an amount of $25 million has been allocated for capital assistance to India.
Discussions have been proceeding with the Indian government on the projects which might be financed out of this grant. I am now in a position to inform the house that Canada has agreed to provide the following economic assistance to India under our Colombo plan program for 1960-61: Wheat to the value of $7 million; aluminum, copper and nickel to the value of $11.7 million; a final allocation for completion of the Canada-India atomic reactor in the amount of $600,000; an initial allocation of $3J million for stage 3 of the Kundah hydroelectric project.
Our agreement to these allocations brings Canadian Colombo plan assistance to India already approved under 1960-61 appropriations to a total of $22.8 million.
The wheat has already been shipped in order to have it cleared from Canadian ports before freeze-up on the St. Lawrence seaway. Arrangements are being made to have the non-ferrous metals shipped without delay.
As is the usual practice in the case of commodities, the Indian government has agreed to set aside counterpart funds in local currency equivalent to the value of the Canadian grant. These counterpart funds will be spent on economic development projects in India to be agreed upon between the two governments. The Canadian wheat will of course be most helpful to India in meeting the food requirements of her growing population which cannot be met from local sources. The metals will assist Indian industry to maintain production and enable development plans to go forward in the face of an acute shortage of foreign exchange.
The Canada-India atomic reactor near Bombay has now been completed, and the Minister of Veterans Affairs represented Canada at the inaugural ceremonies which were held on January 16. The allocation of $600,000 to this project in the current fiscal year is required to cover final expenditures on the Canadian share of the cost of the reactor.
Canada's participation in stage 3 of the Kundah hydroelectric project in Madras state represents a continuation of Canadian interest in this major Indian development scheme, since we have already made a substantial

Colombo Plan Assistance to India contribution to stages 1 and 2. The first two stages were formally inaugurated yesterday, January 13, and the Minister of Veterans Affairs also represented Canada at these ceremonies. Additional power from the Kun-dah project is urgently required for agricultural and industrial development in south India. Canada has, therefore, agreed to provide Canadian equipment, material and engineering services representing the foreign exchange costs of the third stage of Kundah.
This year's allocation of $3.5 million will cover the first instalment of the Canadian contribution and, subject to the appropriation of funds by parliament, further allocations will be made in future years up to an estimated total of $22 million. In addition, Canada has agreed that India should use counterpart funds to the equivalent of $25 million, accruing from the sales of Canadian commodities previously provided to India, to defray the local costs of the Kundah scheme.

He said: This bill, Mr. Speaker, is not a new one in this house. As a matter of fact I have moved this kind of bill now every year since about 1954. After having presented this proposition to parliament in the years immediately prior to 1956 I was able to get a great deal of support across the nation and a good deal of support from members of parliament, and as a result of growing public opinion at that time the government of the day took some steps toward controlling the interest rates charged by small loans companies on particular loan arrangements.
This is a very important question. It is something that affects hundreds of thousands of Canadians, and it would be of benefit to the thousands of families and the tens of thousands of people in this country who are on very low incomes.
The purpose of the bill, Mr. Speaker, is very simple. It would set by law-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I wonder whether I might interrupt the hon. member and ask for better attention. There is a great deal of conversation and shuffling going on while the house settles down to debate. I hope hon. members will give their attention to the hon. member who has the floor.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was saying the purpose of the bill is very simple. It would provide a statutory limit of 12 per cent on all interest rates charged in this country. As I was saying, in 1956 parliament took action to control within a certain range the interest rates set by small loans companies. The area of control affected by the measure of that day was all loans made by small loans companies up to a maximum of $1,500, and the

limits on the interest rates were set as follows, as found in the act:
The cost of a loan shall not exceed the aggregate of
(a)	2 per cent per month on any part of the unpaid principal balance not exceeding $300,
(b)	1 per cent per month on any part of the unpaid principal balance exceeding $300 but not exceeding $1,000, and
(c)	One half of one per cent per month on any remainder of the unpaid principal balance exceeding $1,000.
By this means there was a reduction in the interest rates that might be charged by small loans companies. Even with these changes in the interest rates, however, the business of the small loans companies has flourished. Business done by small loans companies in 1956 amounted to $343 million, and loans outstanding by small loans companies in September of last year amounted to $490 million. So, although there was a slight reduction in interest rates, these companies have flourished, have increased their business and have in no way been harmed by the measure that was passed at that time.
As the years have gone by the effect of this particular measure has been lessened because more and more small loans companies are going into the field of loans in excess of $1,500, and a small loans company making a loan in excess of $1,500 is able to charge any interest rate set forth by agreement, because loans larger than $1,500 do not come under the provisions of the act of parliament.
One of the purposes, therefore, of this particular measure is to bring under control all interest rates charged by small loans companies, and not leave control merely within the area up to $1,500. The whole purpose of the bill, of course, is much broader than this. It would apply to lending rates and interest charges by any loan company, by any firm providing instalment credit or by any individual making a loan.
The field of personal credit is exceedingly important in this country, is exceedingly large and is steadily growing. According to the Bank of Canada statistical summary for September, 1960 the total amount of money now on loan to consumers by finance companies and retail dealers comes to $2,253 million. For quite a period during 1956 and 1957 the amount of instalment or consumer credit in this country was relatively stable, but since 1957 there has been a steady, increasing growth in consumer credit. In 1957 credit in this field amounted to $1,968 million. In 1958 the figure was $2,030 million, in 1959 $2,205 million and in September, 1960, the latest figure available, $2,253 million.
Therefore the area of credit to which the bill would apply is steadily growing and is likely to continue to grow in the future, I 90205-6-78
Interest Act
suggest, even though we are in a very serious recession at the present time. I think the fact of the matter is that many people who have very little money and very little income are forced in such circumstances to go to small loans companies; therefore business in this particular field may increase at a time when there is very widespread unemployment.
The bill would apply to all the major fields of consumer credit. It would apply to credit obtained when financing automobiles. The general rate of interest charged on automobile financing is in the neighbourhood of 16 per cent to 19 per cent. These are the rates charged by the ordinary acceptance corporations doing business in this field. However, there are other fringe companies, smaller companies, fly by night companies, that are charging much higher rates, some of them fabulous and extortionate, and I will refer to this later.
The bill would apply to all instalment credit provided by retail firms doing business on an instalment basis. This is a very important part of credit in Canada, and it is running now in the neighbourhood of $258 million. Companies that sell goods on instalment credit are allowed by law to charge any interest rate they wish to apply to the particular purchase that is made. These interest rates range anywhere from 20 per cent to 50 per cent or more. Some of the large mail order houses in this country, Eaton's, Simpsons-Sears and others, very frequently charge rates of 15 per cent to 20 per cent, and the highest rate charged by Eaton's and Simpsons-Sears works out to 54 per cent per year, a fabulous rate for such reputable firms to be charging on this kind of credit.

I am on another point altogether. I cannot understand the thin skin of members opposite when it comes to dealing with the question of the loan sharks, the racketeers, these people who have fleeced innocent Canadians by charging extortionate interest rates, thereby ruining the lives of many Canadians. I have ample evidence on my desk to support this statement, and I intend to refer to it. I do not understand, for the life of me, why the government does not take some action in this field. Why does the government allow interest rates which are legal-I am not questioning their legality- in this country but which are a disgrace to the nation? These interest rates have been and are being charged.
I have in my hand a copy of Liberty magazine for August, 1959. It contains a long story entitled "How Loan Sharks Put The Bite On". On page 58 an example is given of a Mr. and Mrs. Bert Thompson of Toronto, who paid $878.50 for a car they never owned. They made a down payment of $400 on the car and signed a contract to pay the rest at $36 a month. They paid $618 and had the car just six months. They then turned the car back because they were unable to meet their payments. The car was subsequently sold, and in spite of the large sum of money that had been paid, the Thompsons were left owing a balance of $262.50. I have not the time to give all the references in this article to this particular case, but it shows just what fabulous charges are made by some companies in this field.
I have in my hand an article that appeared in the Globe and Mail of April 28, 1960, entitled "Oakville Man Forced into Paying 87 Per Cent Interest on Second Mortgage". I ask hon. members opposite if they like this. I ask them if they are in favour of it. I ask them if they are opposed to this kind of legalized gangsterism. If they are, why do they not do something about it? The article goes on to say this:
Reports of bonus payments for second mortgages in the Oakville-Trafalgar area brought to light yesterday the case of an Oakville man who was forced to pay effective costs of 87 per cent on a second mortgage for a three-year period.
Three years ago, Edward Waddington went to his lawyer to make arrangements for the down payment on his new home. He had $2,000 in cash, and needed to raise $1,680 more on a second mortgage to make up the total required of $3,680.
"When the mortgage came through, it was for $2,700," Mr. Waddington said, "bearing an interest rate of 6 per cent per annum."

Interest Act
"I thought when I got the papers that it was a typographical error," he continued, "that they had put down $2,700 instead of $1,700, but it wasn't."
Next month, when Mr. Waddington pays his final payment on his second mortgage, he will have repaid $3,186, or 187 per cent of the amount of money he actually got-$1,680.
Experts in the field of real estate report this fantastic cost for a second mortgage was probably not uncommon.
Are the members of the Conservative party in this house in favour of allowing a legal extortionate rate of 87 per cent, as in this example, to be continued in this country? Liberty magazine, the Globe and Mail and the Toronto Daily Star have all given a good deal of thought and publicity to this important problem. Pierre Berton had a series of articles in the Toronto Star in May of 1960. I have an example that I should like to put on the record, and I think it shows just how far some of these gangsters are prepared to go in extorting heavy charges from unsuspecting people. On May 2, 1960 Pierre Berton had this to say in part in one of his articles:
When he-
That is a certain person wishing a loan, namely a Mr. Huider.
-entered Quay Funding's offices he had two mortgages on his home. One had a year to run. The other was not due for almost three years. The total amount he owed on both mortgages was $6,130.19.
When the Lundy-Solnik company was through with him, Mr. Huider had two brand new mortgages on his house. And now he owed $8,795.
In order to get $200 in cash, Mr. Huider allowed Quay Funding to negotiate two new mortgages to replace two old ones. The "finance charges" for this transaction totalled $2,300. In addition, "recording charges" totalled $190. In addition, Mr. Huider must pay interest at per cent and 12 per cent, respectively, on the total value of the mortgages plus all the added charges.
This works out to a real interest rate of 18.3 per cent on his new first mortgage and a real interest rate of 34 per cent on his new second mortgage.
And all Mr. Huider has to show for this is $200 in cash from the people he asked to be his friend.
I'll repeat this for the benefit of those in the back who may not have thought they heard me distinctly:
Mr. Huider got exactly $200, plus the nebulous advantage of a slightly extended period in which to pay his debt. In January, he owed $2,665 more on his house than he owed in December. His monthly payments and his interest rates are now higher than they were before he applied for his loan.
I find this almost unbelievable, but I have the loan agreements and the reporting letter from Quay Funding before me, and I have had the mortgages checked. Mr. Huider is only dimly aware of what has happened. He still does not know what his real interest rates are.
There is something else, alas, that Mr. Huider is not aware of. His loan agreements call for him to make monthly payments of $90. This means that, in four years, when these new, expensive mortgages come due, Mr. Huider will have paid some $4,300 to the Lundy-Solnik firm.

Yet he will still owe more on his house then than he did when he first applied for a loan.
Last December he owed $6,130. Four Decembers from now, if he pays at this rate, he will owe about $7,300. He is paying more than 1,000 per cent interest per annum on his $200.
I ask my hon. friends opposite if they think they are justified in allowing this kind of extortionate practice to continue in our country. I think the government should take action in this field, Mr. Speaker. If the government took action in this field I think there would be other means by which credit could be obtained. If a few of these loan sharks decided that they did not wish to continue in business I would say good riddance, because it would be better to have firms charging 1,000 per cent interest out of business than in business continuing to charge such fabulous rates of interest.
We have credit unions which are doing a good job and which can do an even better job. We have in this country banks which, according to law, can make loans with an interest rate up to 6 per cent. I give the banks credit for having tried in recent years to develop their small loans field at a more rapid rate. I feel that some of the pressure and some of the publicity that has come from discussion in parliament have been instrumental in bringing the banks to exert a greater effort in this field. But it is also a fact, in my judgment, that the banks have cut some corners today by methods that are certainly not established as being legal, in order to bring about for themselves a much higher interest rate than the 6 per cent set forth in the Bank Act. There is on the record and there has been for sometime evidence that the rates are 9 per cent, 10 per cent or 11 per cent. I refer to the effective rates.
I have had sent to me an unsigned letter, but I should be happy to show it to anybody in the house. It sets forth in a detailed way the charges now being made by the Bank of Nova Scotia in the small loans field. The writer of this letter, whoever he may be, has come to the conclusion that the rates are some 12.6 per cent. I suggest that the government should have this practice checked and should inform the house whether in fact these rates are being charged. Certainly they are cutting corners. Certainly they are charging rates in excess of 6 per cent.

We want action; we want the government to do something. I do not know why the government will not move in this field. They
Interest Act
claim they are not afraid to bring forth legislation that will mean a new Canadianism. They are provoking Canadianism all the time. If they are doing this in a real and effective sense they should not be afraid to bring in legislation that will limit the charges that are made by finance companies in our country, since approximately 70 per cent of the business done by finance companies is done by companies that are wholly owned in the United States.
Why should we allow Canadian companies or any other companies the right to levy these extortionate rates of interest? This field is dominated by United States corporations. A government that has the attitude which this government has to outside capital from the United States surely should not be backward in doing the right thing, affecting all companies in this field, more particularly since 70 per cent of the business is in the hands of companies wholly owned in the United States.
I have given examples of some of the fabulous rates of interest that are being charged in this country. The thing that amazes me is that they are being charged in a legal manner, that this government has taken no steps to control these charges. I know it is going to be said that property and civil rights belong to the provinces, but long ago it was established that interest rates are under the control of this parliament, and every other charge that is associated with a given transaction has been interpreted as being an interest charge. Therefore this government has the right to legislate in this field.
I suggest that this government, badly in need of political support as it is at this time, badly in need of some moves that will carry some popular support, could do nothing better than extend the area of interest control and limit the interest rates along the lines I have suggested.
The banks can do a better job, the credit unions can do a better job, a bigger job. They are capable of doing it. I suggest that to allow a maximum rate of 12 per cent is allowing a rate, if anything, too high, but a rate surely that is adequate for normal, legitimate, efficient businesses to carry on their operations and make a return on those operations.

I challenge the government to take off the whip. It is of importance in normal times; it is of greater importance when hundreds of thousands of Canadians have lost their jobs, when people are on very low incomes and may be forced, through family difficulties, into the hands of these loan sharks who can ruin them financially for the rest of their lives.

I have had the privilege of speaking on this bill on two or three previous occasions. Like hon. members from the other side of the house who have introduced this bill, I have been able to bring to the attention of this house and the country very serious instances where people have misused the second mortgage market. Perhaps as a result of having spoken in this house I have been the recipient of a great deal of literature pro and con this question. I must confess that the more I study this subject the more complicated it seems and the more confused I become. It is not quite as simple as the hon. member has stated.
I would like, in all fairness, before I deal with this matter to answer in part some of the things that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has stated. He has pointed out, and I think quite properly, some of the abuses that have been prevalent in the second mortgage field. He knows that I have brought similar instances before this house. But I think in all fairness he must admit that in

1960 legislation was passed in the province of Ontario, in an act known as the Ontario mortgage brokers act, where it is set out and required that people who are registering mortgages must set out in detail what are the interest rate, the bonuses, and so on. It is hoped that this will overcome the difficulties of people not knowing what they are signing. If they are over 21 years of age, can read and go to their lawyer, they can be advised. But if they refuse to do those things it is going to be difficult for us to help them.
That was one step in this direction, and it was a step within the jurisdiction of the provincial government. That is what the provincial government is doing. What is more, they are still investigating other instances of these irregularities that have been brought to their attention perhaps by members of this house and by writers such as Pierre Berton. I must advise this house that they are not sitting idle and letting these things go by. Incidentally, it is a Conservative government that is doing it.

speechtext:
The hon. member says "They are allowing it to be done". They are doing whatever they can in their power to stop these practices. One of the difficulties confronting us today is the lack of recognition on the part of many people of the problems and complications involved in economic questions. The hon. member for Assiniboia brings forward many proposals, but until he realizes the complications involved and stops tarring everybody with the same brush his suggestions will be of no value in solving the problem.
The subject of interest and interest rates has been discussed many times in this house. As the result of discussions in years gone by we have on our statute books the Small Loans Act which came into effect in 1938-39 and was amended in 1956. There is also the Pawnbrokers Act and the Interest Act. What we are now dealing with are the weaknesses in this legislation which permit certain companies without ethics to prey on those who need money.
In dealing with this problem we have to consider what is the thing we call money. Some people consider it a commodity, others a means of facilitating trade, and still others consider it to be both. Interest rates are usually set by competition, the natural level at which money can be obtained in normal competition. When money is in short supply interest rates go up. Interest rates also vary in accordance with the risks involved. Hence, rates of interest on loans with collateral security are less than those without security,

and interest rates on first mortgages are less than on second and third mortgages. These are basic assumptions.
The problem of interest rates is further complicated by monetary policy. In times of threatening inflation those who control the monetary policy encourage high interest rates in order to discourage the demand for money. Also, if money is in short supply interest rates may be increased by the demand. If there is too much money in circulation which is causing inflation there is a tendency for monetary authorities to encourage high interest rates. The more we study the problem the more confused we become and the more complicated we realize it is. A simple declaration by act of parliament that the rate of interest should not be higher than 12 per cent seems destined to failure when we consider the sense of balance of our complex economy.
The hon. member for Assiniboia in drafting this bill did not direct his attention to the economic theories behind the various forces which influence the rate of interest. The hon. gentleman, like many of us, is more impressed by and concerned with the abuses of greedy moneylenders. The buying public, being unaware and trusting, fall prey to encouragement to increase their debt, and thus overanxious consumers become committed to various loans.
This bill is an expression of a desire to protect people. It is prompted by the same motive which prompted the introduction of the other acts to which I referred which are on our statute books for the protection of the public. It is perhaps for the same reasons that the province of Ontario recently passed an act to protect people who have been involved in second mortgages and is continuing its investigation of the activities of certain unscrupulous moneylenders.
The sponsor of this bill appears to share the hope that people who wish to borrow on future earnings to pay for present needs should be able to do so at a lesser cost. Hence we are faced with two different approaches which are seemingly contradictory and conflicting. If we were to adopt the principle that people should be able to borrow all they want to buy whatever they wish and pay only a low rate of interest, one way to do this would be to create more money so that the money supply would be sufficient to meet the demand and interest rates would remain naturally low in a competitive market. On the other hand the government could go directly into the lending business and create the money it wished to loan at a low rate of interest.
Interest Act
I am not an economist. I can, however, foresee some of the consequences of a course of action of this nature on the value of our dollar. We would probably wind up with greater confusion, and perhaps we would create a greater hardship on the people we are seeking to assist.
However much we may speculate and dream about these things, we have to face the realities of the situation. We cannot create money at will, nor can we in our every day needs and requirements simply go out and buy everything we see just because we want it. We have to buy things in accordance with our needs and means. We should be astute enough as individuals not to sign contracts which are averse to us. If we do not know what these contracts mean or involve, we should be intelligent enough to have a friend or lawyer check them over. This is an important subject because of the implications it has relating to our whole economy.
The hon. member for Assiniboia set out some figures illustrating the scope of consumer credit in our Canadian communities. The dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin of November 16, 1960 shows that the balances outstanding on the books of sales finance companies at the end of September amounted to $1,245,500,000. Outstanding balances on consumer goods at the end of September were $849,200,000. Bank loans at the end of October last were $6,257,000,000.
In July of 1960 United States consumer credit stood at $53.5 billion. John Kenneth Galbraith in his recent book "The Affluent Society", page 201, sets out some interesting figures relating to the United States economy which may have some general application here. Between 1952 and 1956 total consumer loans increased from $27.4 billion to $41.7 billion, or by 53 per cent. In that time the disposable income increased by only 21 per cent. In other words the people of the United States seemed to be spending more money than they had available.
In the period to which I referred instalment credit increased by 63 per cent and that for automobiles by nearly 100 per cent. In 1955 one family in four with an income of between $3,000 and $4,000 bought automobiles, 69 per cent of them on credit. One family in three with an income between $4,000 and $5,000 bought automobiles, 66 per cent on credit. Those with income in excess of $10,000, in the majority, paid cash for their automobile purchases. There is no indication, however, as to whether some of these seeming cash transactions were in fact purchases made with cash borrowed elsewhere unknown to the seller of the automobile.
Both in our economy and that of the United States the question of consumer credit

Interest Act
is of great importance. Because of that fact the finance and mortgage companies have moved in to fill a need. We cannot deny that there is a need, nor can we deny that there have been abuses. It is the duty of the government to study these things and try to eliminate the abuses. I differ from the hon. member for Assiniboia, who takes the examples of the abuses and then proceeds to paint everybody in the business with the same brush. I think he is doing a disfavour to those who are giving a service in the provision of consumer credit.
The hon. gentleman pointed out two or three groups that he feels can handle this better than others. But even at that perhaps he has been too broad in his accusations. I am not saying that the instances he gave are wrong, but I feel that they do not reflect the practices of the majority of those who are in the consumer credit business.
Before we come to the conclusion that 12 per cent is the easy way out of the difficulty and is the be-all and end-all, we have to realize that in coming to that conclusion there are costs involved. There are certain charges, and this bill, regardless of what the hon. member for Assiniboia says, cannot cover them. The hon. member made the statement, and I question it, that every charge can be interpreted as an interest rate. Unfortunately I have not the law before me, but it is my understanding that when the Small Loans Act was enacted and the control of charges was included in the act it was done with the permission of the provinces concerned. The hon. member shakes his head. I have no way of repudiating it; we will have to leave that for future examination.

speechtext: I wonder whether I may just say something to the hon. member. My statement, at least in part, was based on the evidence given by the deputy minister of justice before the banking and commerce committee back in 1956, when, at one place in the evidence in answer to a series of questions, he made it perfectly clear that in his view the federal government had the power to control all charges because that power flows from the undisputed power of the federal government to control interest charges, and it would not be controlling the rates if the government controlled the interest rate and a company could charge what was in fact a higher rate by calling it something else.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I think that points up the difficulty we are in, when we say that 12 per cent would be the most that could be charged. If other charges and costs amounted to 10 per cent of the 12 per cent, the interest

would be only 2 per cent. If we were to add up the sum total of the cost to the person obtaining the loan under those conditions, it would not be any more than 12 per cent. We might be able to do that indirectly, but this brings up the point as to how practical it would be, because for some loans and in some places the charges for services are greater. It may be doing indirectly what you cannot do directly. This points out the constitutional difficulty.
As I say, in some provinces they are going as far as they can, and what they need is assistance. This sort of thing should not be done by the provinces and the dominion separately. I think the time has come when this whole matter, like many other matters in our economy and in relation to our constitution, must be dealt with by the provinces and the dominion together if we are to have effective legislation to meet the problem.
The hon. member mentioned a department store charging 40 per cent or 50 per cent on a purchase. That could be worked out in this way. Someone purchases something in a store for $30 and has to make his payments over a three months period at $10 a month. He is charged $2 interest. This amounts to 40 per cent per annum. Without explanation this seems to be an enormous charge, but to the person buying the article the $2 does not amount to very much, and he feels it is worth it. The same thing can be said of service given to a loan which costs $2 or something of that order. The loan is small. We cannot be too dogmatic in saying that the charges should be 12 per cent.
If the hon. member would read the act in conjunction with his bill, Bill No. C-20, he would realize that there is an anomaly there, because in one section of the act it is said that on a loan of $1,000 to $1,500 the total cost of the loan is less than 1 per cent per month, whereas in Bill No. C-3 the interest rate is 1 per cent per month. There is an anomaly there.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: The rate is lower for the portion of the loan between $1,000 and $1,500 than is provided in this bill.

speechtext:
If you look at the statistics of the loans made you will see there are fewer loans in that field between $1,000 and $1,500. This is not so much because people do not want them in that amount but because finance companies do not find it profitable to make loans in that field. The field of loans over $1,500 is more profitable.
These are some of the difficulties connected with interest rates. There are various ways in which to set interest rates. You may have a 6 per cent interest rate on a monthly

instalment contract. It could be 6 per cent per annum or it could be a 6 per cent flat add-on rate, or a flat 6 per cent discount rate. You may borrow $100 and pay 6 per cent, but you receive only $94. Therefore, in effect you are paying on that $94 almost 12 per cent. It becomes very complicated when you try to calculate actually what is the interest rate. That is what I am trying to point out to the hon. member. It is not as simple as he appears to make it to be. That is why it is most difficult to control these things.
Perhaps hon. members would be interested in knowing who are the people who make these purchases, or who purchase by this method. Let me give their occupations. According to a pamphlet put out by the federated council of sales finance companies, with headquarters in Ottawa, 13 per cent of the loans are made by proprietary and managerial groups; 5.9 per cent by professional people; 4.1 per cent by armed forces personnel; 6.2 per cent by farmers, fishermen and lumbermen; 5.8 per cent by salesmen and agents; 50.3 per cent by skilled and semiskilled labour; and 14.7 per cent by clerical people and others. That gives a sort of crosssection of the people who need this assistance, and indicates its importance.
The question has sometimes been brought up whether we need regulations. Of course we do, and I should like to refer to an example in the United States. In a pamphlet called "Consumer Credit Facts For You", published by the bureau of business research, Western Reserve University, there is the following on page 16:
Legislation has an important influence on maximum rates. Only five states set maximum rates for retail instalment financing transactions. In these states maximum rates vary from 24 per cent on new cars to 43 per cent on used cars. Evidence collected by legislative bodies indicates that corresponding maximums in uncontrolled states are at least 120 to 275 per cent.
So there is merit in legislation. We do not deny that, and there is all sorts of proof of it. The question is how best to regulate this field. The fact is that this problem raises many questions. Recently I received a pamphlet, which perhaps many hon. members also received, from Saunders Cameron Limited, 55 Yonge street, Toronto, containing suggestions concerning a royal commis-mission on Canadian monetary matters. Under the heading "Trust and Loan Companies" certain questions are raised which I think indicate that this is not a simple matter. Many people more learned than ourselves with respect to economic conditions are raising questions. The author of the pamphlet has this to say:
Are the trust and loan companies satisfactorily fulfilling the place of the English or United States
Interest Act
building and loan societies in Canada? Should there be close ties between such companies and chartered banks? Should there be any provision for Bank of Canada control over trust and loan companies and, if so, how can it be applied to companies under both federal and provincial charter? Many more questions can be imagined which should shed light on the place of these institutions in our structure.
With respect to finance companies this statement is made:
Here we enter an area of conflict between the federal powers over interest rates and provincial powers over property and civil rights which might cover conditional sale agreements. Should the Bank of Canada be given powers over these companies and how they may be operated? How can companies with access to foreign funds be satisfactorily controlled on the same basis as domestic concerns? Would some form of taxation, exempting companies which are under or place themselves under federal jurisdiction, induce companies dealing in conditional sale agreements to operate in the same manner as loan companies where there are rules respecting interest rates, etc.?
What about consumer credit interest rates? Do they affect the individual's willingness to borrow? Should they be spelled out as an annual rate of interest, or should it be recognized that some charges are legitimately made for investigation, etc., and morally not a form of interest? Are there abuses and how may they be prevented?
I think this points out the difficulty of the situation and the need of a genuine investigation into the matter. I think that in all legislation dealing with this matter we have to recognize the philosophy that we cannot legislate for, shall I say, the lack of morals and poor ethics of some people in our society. There is a limit to which we can go in protecting people. We can set up ground rules, but we cannot legislate that a person be good when he does not want to be good. If he wants to be a crook he will do all he can to get around the rules that we make.
The greatest protection that we might have in this field would be a better ethical code on the part of those involved in these activities. A similar question was raised in the winter edition of "The Canadian Banker", in which it is said in effect that if businessmen want to keep the government out of business through legislation, if they want to prevent the government from interfering with the details of their day to day business, they will have to improve the ethical code under which they operate because as they become less ethical in their business operations they invite the government to come into the field to try to control them.
I think that is perhaps pretty much the situation in the matter of consumer credit today. Many of these people have been unethical. We can only go so far in establishing rules, but there must be an ethical code established by responsible companies in the field and they should help the government to ferret out and put out of business those

Interest Act
people who do not adhere to an ethical code. On page 29 of the article, which is written by Mr. A. Beedle, the author comes to these conclusions. I quote in part:
Business should therefore:
(1)	Be willing to let government share in the guardianship of business conscience. Some desirable results can only be obtained through government action. State action acts as a stimulant of conscience. Business, however, should try to see that government does not entirely usurp its role. Business should not abdicate its role. Achieving this balance may be delicate ...
(2)	It should recognize and accept the beneficial aspects of countervailing powers and be willing to adopt readily measures for the common good, instead of regarding countervailing powers as always representing detrimental interests.
(4)	It should not ignore religion. It does not have to back all Moral Re-Armament groups; it does not have to hand its conscience over to the religious authorities; but it should be willing to adopt as practical politics those measures of which it approves. It is too prone at the moment to pay mere lip service to or completely ignore religious principles.
(5)	Above all it should educate and train in economic statesmanship. It should support studies in the universities and other academic institutions. It should set up its own study groups. It should make pronouncements on moral issues.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize that the bringing forward of this bill by the hon. member for Assiniboia has provided an opportunity to disclose to the public those abuses that are prevalent and need to be rooted out. In bringing this matter before the house he has brought forward something that needs a great deal of discussion, and I think the debate should impress upon the government the need of further study as to the role of interest in our economy.
Although the purpose is laudable and the principle is simple, I feel that the application of the bill is not as simple as it may appear on the surface, but that should not deter us from studying the matter and bringing people here who know all the implications of interest with respect to the economy. We should be able to devise some method of control that is not too rigid and yet will be effective in dealing with those people who like to live by sponging off others who cannot afford it, people who do not know how to protect themselves, people who are in unfortunate circumstances not always through their own fault. They should, in some way, be protected. I agree in this respect with the sponsor of the bill, and to that end I have, on occasion, brought before this house examples of the things I felt were wrong, especially in the second mortgage market. I believe this has borne some fruit because I know some investigations have taken place in Ontario. The Ontario department has moved to remedy that situation and they are still investigating those who have been unconscionable in their activities.

I should like to urge upon our government and our cabinet the making of a study of the implications of the interest rate as it relates to the consumer credit field, that vast field in which people are dependent upon loans to assist them in buying the things they need. I think we should say the things they need and not what they want because they cannot afford everything they want. I believe the government should ascertain that these institutions which need to fulfil a vital role are filling that role at not too great an expense to those who need their services.

Mr. Speaker, I would preface my remarks by stating my sympathy with the point of view of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) who has pointed out the hardships people have to sustain as a result of the unethical and unscrupulous practices of these loan sharks and moneylenders in a field which has done so much to contribute to human unhappiness. I wonder if the loan companies who are under discussion here today because of the interest rates they charge had not filled this area in the money lending market, it would not have fallen to more unscrupulous and unethical operators?
This bill, presented by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is becoming an annual old friend. I do not doubt the honesty or sincerity of purpose of my hon. friend, and I commend the suggestion of the hon. member for Davenport that the situation would bear detailed study by a committee of this house from time to time. The great value of such a study would be that arguments could be refuted by the reputable people in this industry, by facts and figures, by specific cases and especially in terms of their own public relations.
All of us are aware of the very seductive advertising that has become a prelude to every Christmas and which is to some extent inflated and misleading to those who are on the receiving end. These people, not knowing better, soon find themselves lured to attend at one of these offices where they are offered a consolidation of their Christmas debts. I trust they are told not only what the net loan will be but what the gross cost of the loan may ultimately be. I am assured by reputable members of the industry that this is indeed their approach and that the interest rate is clearly disclosed. In many cases, it is disclosed in the area of the signature. I only hope the supplementary information is given, namely that you are borrowing $300 but you will be expected to pay $350 or $375 or whatever it may be. I have not precisely calculated that amount, I have only guessed at it.

The hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out that these companies have been flourishing since 1956. I think that was the date he used. I have before me a report from the department of insurance for the year ending December 31, 1959 which contains a chart listing the 77 finance companies. Of these 77 companies, 14 showed a loss and 63 showed a profit. There were 24 companies that had a profit of less than $10,000; nine had a profit of less than $20,000. Only 30 out of the 77 loan companies made a profit in excess of $20,000. This does not reflect the rosy picture of pyramiding profits the hon. member was pointing out in his general remarks, but there are some companies-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I was glad to note that my friend the hon. member for Davenport alluded to the situation where the interest rate was said to be 54 per cent. I am sure that my friend the hon. member for Assiniboia was being quite honest and true when he said that that interest rate was computed on an extremely small amount of money with a monthly charge over a period of perhaps three or four months. But that certainly is misleading as far as the major retail companies are concerned to suggest that they are charging interest rates at that level because by and large, on charge accounts and so on, it is not their custom to charge any interest rate whatsoever.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I would say as far as retail companies are concerned. The other point I want to come to has to do with the fact that this industry has grown to a point where there are 150 financial houses across the country and over 550 branches. If we take into consideration the fact that each branch might conceivably employ ten people, we arrive at a substantial number of employees, namely a minimum of 5,500 employees in this industry across the nation. Hence, if we were to pass this bill in its present form I would think the tendency in the industry, because of their high risk factor and the cost of the multiplicity of loans on a small quantum basis which results in heavy services and other charges, would be that these companies would not be able to continue in business, with the consequent loss of employment across the nation.

Interest Act
I have always been of the opinion that given honest service with good public relations they have a gap to fill in the economy and that they fill it very usefully.
My friend the hon. member for Assiniboia referred to the many legislative studies that have taken place over the years both in the Senate and the House of Commons banking and commerce committees. I want to quote in part some of the conclusions that came out of these committee hearings up to the time the present act was passed. As an authority for this quotation I am using the pamphlet entitled "Consumer loans in Canada". At page 3 these five conclusions are stated:
1.	-our modern economy creates a need for small-sum, short term loans to wage-earners and salaried people.
2.	-the demand will be met, either by legal and supervised agencies or by unlicensed lenders at unregulated rates.
3.	-the actual cost of making and servicing such loans far exceeded the 12 per cent per annum provision of the then existing Money-Lender's Act.
4.	[DOT]-if legal, supervised service was to be provided, the permitted maximum charge-to cover every element of cost, including interest-must be adequate to enable efficient management to earn sufficient profit to attract enough capital.
5.	-prohibitory legislation would be ineffective and would result only in forcing needy borrowers into the hands of unlicensed lenders.
In the Interest Act in part I there is a clause which reads as follows:
5. No person shall transact the business of a moneylender unless such person has first obtained from the minister a licence: but this section does not apply to a moneylender the cost of whose loans does not in any case exceed an amount equivalent to 1 per cent per month on the unpaid principal balance thereof.
It is obvious that consumer lenders would not take out licences and accept the many restrictive provisions of the Small Loans Act unless the Interest Act were further amended to specifically exclude them from its rate requirement. If there are no licensees there are no annual reports, no examination of lenders' books and records and no restriction of such matters as length of contract, reduction in charges for prepaid accounts, minimum charges, and many other features which now offer excellent protection to the borrowing public. The result would be a long step backward in the history of borrowing and lending in Canada, and I think this would be a mistake of the first magnitude.
Consumer lenders actively advocated a small loans law and accepted the terms and conditions of the Small Loans Act in 1939. They have not seriously objected to it since then, mainly because the act provides a rate of charge higher than for other kinds of lending in recognition of the higher costs involved in making personal instalment loans. These lenders may feel differently about a

definition of interest as broad as that suggested in Bill No. C-3 if the statutory rate is reduced to the point that it becomes impossible to earn a profit.
Since the Interest Act covers a much wider field than the Small Loans Act there will no doubt be many other kinds of lenders who will find such a definition of interest unpalatable. For example, loans on real estate often incur heavy expenses for inquiries, appraisals, recording fees, commissions, et cetera. If these must be lumped into one total charge along with the rate of interest on the loan as a 1 per cent per month maximum it would certainly seriously slow down the rate of mortgage lending, especially on secondary security.
This mortgage problem in the lending field -I refer to second and third mortgages- was brought to the attention of the house by my friend the hon. member for Davenport and it points to a real and difficult situation and the need for supervision of loans of this nature by way of some sort of provincial act such as that which is now on the books in the province of Ontario which should point a good example to the other provinces in Canada. As a lawyer I have dealt with many people who were confronted with this situation of being overly mortgaged, with 20 per cent to 30 per cent discount on second and third mortgages, and to have suddenly found themselves out of work and unable to meet the payments they found that their equity in their home had been swallowed up, with the net result that they lost their home and their place of living at an extremely difficult time when they are in financial straits.
This kind of legislation is of great credit to the province of Ontario, and of course that province has a Conservative government. This is the kind of legislation that I believe should be followed by all the other provinces of our nation. I have here the Bank of Montreal Business Review issue of September 26, 1960, which I think contains a rather good definition of consumer credit:
Consumer credit is generally regarded as consisting of contractual obligations entered into by individuals, as consumers but not as house buyers, for personal rather than business reasons. As such it includes indebtedness incurred in the form of charge accounts, or commitments to pay for goods and services by instalments, or personal cash borrowings without attendant collateral in the form of stocks and bonds.
Prior to world war II there were only $400 million outstanding in Canada in consumer credit. By 1943, due to the exigencies of the second world war, the production especially of household goods, and so on, this dropped to $200 million. By 1946 it advanced to $400 million again and it had passed the $1 billion

mark by 1950. It was again restricted during the Korean war, for obvious reasons, and ever since has been on the rise until now it stands at $3J billion.
This is a tremendous increase in the field of consumer borrowing, but in my opinion it is rather the sociological trend of our times. People want to have possession of some desirable and useful chattel now and pay for it later. In most cases I am sure they understand the consequences of the charges that ensue by way of interest. But there is that small segment of the public which is drawn into these financial offices, and if these people are not treated with the respect, understanding and sympathy which they deserve they are apt to be committed to a loan to pay for such goods and chattels which they really cannot afford.
In the same Bank of Montreal Business Review there is a table showing consumer credit as a percentage of personal disposable income. I thought it would be of interest to the house to put this table on the record. In 1950 it was 8.3 per cent of personal disposable income; in 1951 it was 6.8 per cent; in 1952 it was 8.9 per cent; in 1953, 10.5 per cent; in 1954, 11.3 per cent; in 1955, 12.6 per cent; in 1956, 13.1 per cent; in 1957, 13 per cent; in 1958, 13.3 per cent. Then in 1959 it rose to 14.1 per cent and in 1960, as at the end of the first quarter-which is the last figure available-it was 13.5 per cent.
At the present time, when there is a slight recession in the economy, consumer credit shows a definite falling off. When times are good it shows a sturdy gain. To suggest, as the hon. member for Assiniboia did, that in times when there is high unemployment- as there is at the moment-the credit companies are in a more advantageous position is quite wrong. These statistics clearly indicate that they are as buoyant as any other business in good times, and their business falls off very substantially when times are not so good.
There are different types of consumer credit. First of all you have the charge account type of credit, which is the short term, almost month by month account and the account is paid at the end of each month. Even though it is not paid until it becomes pretty badly in default, there are no interest charges on it. This type of charge account increased by 50 per cent in 1959 over what it was in 1951 and now represents 13 per cent of total consumer debt, as opposed to 29 per cent in 1951, which is an interesting development.
Then there is instalment credit. This type of credit, instalment buying, by way of contrast to the charge account type of consumer credit, increased 4i times between 1951 and
Interest Act
1959. This aspect of credit is dealt with on page 2 of the Bank of Montreal Business Review, as follows:
The unevenness of annual increases already noted in consumer debt generally has been particularly apparent in instalment credit. Most of the rise since 1951 occurred in the years prior to 1957 when, despite the arrested growth in 1954, instalment debt grew at an annual compound rate of about 25 per cent. In the past two years the rate of increase has been notably lower, averaging less than 4 per cent. Thus, while nearly half of consumer debt was in the form of instalment credit at the end of 1957, the proportion now approximates two fifths.
The third type of consumer credit is personal cash loan. This has become a major component of consumer credit. It started out very slowly in the 1950's and increased in volume until at the present time it represents nearly one half of all the consumer credit in our country. Hence, when you use the chart issued by the superintendent of insurance, probably if one went back to 1951 he would find just a small handful of these finance companies. Today, as I pointed out, there are 77, each of them growing year by year.
It is interesting to know that more than half of the non-farm family units have no consumer debt whatsoever, and one third of these do have liquid cash assets in excess of the amount of their own indebtedness. So that when you look at the whole picture it is not quite so bad as it seems. Assuming that this is really becoming a social change of our day I should like to quote the Radcliffe committee of the United Kingdom which aptly summed up the role of consumer credit in the following terms:
While he (the purchaser) escapes the necessity of saving in advance of his purchases, and draws on the savings of others to finance his investment, the act of repayment restores those savings for other uses, and there remains in the hands of consumers, after the discharge of their obligations, a stock of goods that may be presumed to make as real a contribution to the amenities of life as any other form of investment.
That would appear to indicate that the money being loaned out across the country by these finance companies is in its own way doing good in that it is keeping a substantially growing amount of money in circulation which keeps up the level of consumer purchases and, in its own fashion, contributes to the general buoyancy of our economy.
I wish to quote from a pamphlet called "Facts about consumer loans" prepared by the Househould Finance Corporation which company has been in business in Canada since 1927. The pamphlet points out:
The need for satisfactory sources of small sum loans to wage earners and consumers has only developed in Canada during comparatively recent years, with the change from an agrarian to an industrial economy and the consequent shift of

Interest Act
population from rural to urban area. The resulting dependence of a growing number of people on cash income rather than on the physical products of their own hands, has produced this need. Early laws did not protect borrowers, and many people needing small loans were victimized by unscrupulous lenders charging exorbitant rates.
This condition did not develop as soon in Canada as in the United States, where intensive studies of the problem commenced in 1908. Most active in this field was the Russell Sage foundation, a philanthropic body dedicated to the improvement of social and living conditions.
Studies by the foundation showed that laws limiting interest on all loans regardless of size, were inadequate as far as small loans were concerned, since they only prevented small loans being made legally, and drove people into the hands of the loan sharks. It was also apparent from experiments with the operation of philanthropic lending agencies that the need for small loans could not be met in this manner. The foundation concluded that the only answer was to pass laws which would provide small loan rates low enough to protect borrowers, but high enough to attract sufficient capital to the business to meet the public need. Only by doing this could the borrower be protected.
The foundation received the support of legal lenders, among them Household Finance, and by 1917 the first uniform small loan law had been passed in several states. Since then improved versions of this law have been passed in the majority of states.
In Canada by 1936, it was apparent that a small loan law was necessary, for here, as had happened in the United States the high rate lenders were plying their trade. Realization of this condition led to the passage of the Small Loans Act in 1939-
There was a reason and purpose for these companies coming into existence. The experience here in Canada clearly points to the fact that people were being stung by unethical and unscrupulous operators. The change in our whole economic set-up, the movement of the population from rural to urban centres, higher wage rates, higher employment and the consequent greater amount of cash available to working people led these companies into a field which investigation establishes was clearly needed. Accordingly I cannot agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia when he says that we would be doing the public of Canada a service by accepting the hon. member's proposed bill at face value realizing the constitutional anomalies that were already pointed out in this debate and realizing the conflict between this bill and the existing Small Loans Act even at this level leaving out the provinces entirely.
Before accepting such a measure I feel we should conduct a full and thorough investigation. With that in mind I feel that a more intelligent decision could be reached if all the evidence were placed before the banking and commerce committee. We should take into consideration the fact that the present act has remained relatively unchanged since
[Mr. Chown.f
1936. From the evidence obtained and the witnesses heard we could come to a sober conclusion as a result of having another and very close look at this whole general problem.
In the meantime, it would be difficult for me to support this bill. I do not know how my hon. friend arrived at 12 per cent as a figure for the maximum interest rate. It appears as though he has simply taken the present allowable maximum of 2 per cent per month, chopped it in half and reduced it to 1 per cent and said, "That will do because that is what my friends in the cooperatives and credit unions are charging, and that seems to be a fairly reasonable interest rate".
It is important to remember that those in co-operatives and credit union societies are not coping with such a broad area of risk where you have thousands of small loans in the amount of $200 and $300 apiece thinly spread among hundreds of thousands of people all of which loans have to be serviced, checked and rechecked and pursued when they are in default.
When a loan is in default the lending institution must decide whether it is advisable in terms of the possibility of collection to pursue the account through legal processes. Even if the money is collectible the institution must determine whether or not to pursue it through legal processes and face the consequences of bad public relations.
My hope is that they will find that recourse through the courts, or by way of chattel mortgage through a bailiff and a seizure is an unprofitable move from the standpoint of their general public relations because they should know better than to become involved in that type of situation in the first place. In other words, they have to take a very responsible attitude toward each risk they accept and when a poor risk is discovered they should reflect on the fact that there was bad judgment on their own part before they incur the poor public relations that will follow if they pursue the account through legal processes.
The philosophy that the customer is always right is more applicable to finance companies than to retail stores. No human being can sit back and be happy over the dire results of playing along with a poor risk, and least of all a finance company. I think finance companies are charged with a very grave responsibility in this regard, a responsibility to tell the public the true story of the interest that is being charged, to state with courage the fact that 2 per cent per month means 24 per cent per year, and to look with caution and with care, into the

background of people whom they are servicing and to weigh up the consequences of a default by a person through loss of employment or disaster in the family or any other cause.
If finance companies do not accede to the charge made against them, and accept this very grave and heavy responsibility, then the time will come when they will face the possibility that public clamour will rise to the point where some action will have to be taken, both at the federal and provincial levels, to police those corporations with even greater care than they are policed at the present time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE CEILING ON INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks on this matter will be very brief, as I merely wish to support the principle of Bill C-3, even if I do not fully agree with its terms.
Bill C-3 will, if passed, decree that the maximum interest rate that may be charged by companies or loan institutions be set at 12 per cent.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, as the mover of the bill is none other than the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), who is also leader of a party with socialist tendencies, and who, at least in theory, claims to be able to provide our country with more favourable legislation in the economic field, it is obvious that, in this case, we might have expected something more spectacular.
My purpose in speaking at this time is to submit to the house and to defend the position of the working classes, of the small wage earners.
However, I am not of those who advocate the principle of lending money without interest.
On the contrary, I recognize that if borrowed money is useful to the borrower, it should provide a return to the lender.
Interest Act
I think that if I rent an apartment, a car, or some other article I have to pay something for the wear and tear of the merchandise or premises.
I must admit that credit unions and chartered banks are charging reasonable interest rates in this field and are rendering a great service to their customers.
Unfortunately we cannot say as much with regard to other loan companies regularly established on the market, some of which advertise on television, or on the radio, claiming that they are ready to give tremendous service to people by advancing them the money they need.
First of all, let it be clearly understood that I have nothing to reproach, either directly or indirectly to the management or employees of those companies. Most of them are very honest people, working for modest salaries. Yet, I would state categorically that those companies are doing a disservice to people, in the majority of cases where our fellow-citizens deal with them.
The interest rates charged on the full amount of the loan, or on any outstanding balance for the purchase of an article, on the basis sometimes of a rate of 9 per cent, and even more in some instances, on the total amount, and for the whole period of repayment on purchases paid by monthly instalments, amount to twice the interest rate provided in the contract.
Mr. Speaker, as a member of parliament, I am often visited by some constituents of mine who come and tell me about their financial difficulties. Most of them, after we have discussed their financial troubles, fish out of their pockets what is known in our province as a finance contract. They have borrowed money from lending institutions whose interest rates are exorbitant. Those companies, I can well appreciate, are probably taking greater risks than do our credit unions and our charter banks, but a man would be better off in being refused a loan at a reasonable rate of interest, if it would be too much of a burden to him, than to be granted one at a rate of interest he cannot affort to pay.
Toward the end of 1959, the Bank of Canada had instructed all chartered banks to restrict their credit facilities. And, of course, as a consequence, chartered banks had to curtail loans which they normally grant to their usual borrowers. However, for reasons unknown to me, no restrictions at all were imposed by the Bank of Canada on the companies T have now in mind, with the result

Interest Act
many patrons no longer applied to banks and credit unions and turned to these lending companies which charge higher rates of interest. Consequently low wage earners have had to pay more in interest for money they had borrowed and which, in certain cases, they could have done without.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the services rendered by such companies to people buying cars, furniture and so on. However 1 feel that in proportion to the service rendered, the interest rates charged are far too high.
As I have said, I admit that in some instances lending companies have operated at a loss. In fact the previous speaker mentioned that 14 companies had run into deficits.
Mr. Speaker, it goes without saying that I do not want to suggest that the financial reports of those companies might be doctored. But I wonder whether figures are not somewhat like music and whether it is not possible to make them give off various sounds.
In any case, I wonder how our caisses populates, making loans at 6 and 5 per cent interest in some instances, can manage to accumulate reserves and lend money at rates much lower than those charged by these lending institutions? How is it that in every town and city of every province in this country chartered banks can lend money at reasonable rates and get along, as far as I know, while other lending companies charging twice the same rates are showing a deficit?
Mr. Speaker, it is without any trace of bitterness that I sought to express my humble opinion in this debate about financing and money in Canada.
I happen to come from an area which is rather average, if not downright poor and, as I was saying earlier, I have in many instances witnessed the dire predicament of some of my fellow citizens who had been lured by credit or loan facilities at very heavy rates of interest.
Mr. Speaker, 1 am happy to find that this government is taking action in the sense I have just suggested, as evidenced by the Small Loans Act passed before the Christmas recess. I am sure that this measure will greatly benefit small businesses and provide a reasonable interest rate. I sincerely hope it will be followed by other legislation enabling Canadians in need of credit to secure loans at reasonable rates of interest.
