Mr. Speaker, my first thought on this subject is one of 
some surprise that the official opposition has in effect bowed to the claims of those who claim they are the effective opposition in presenting measures of this sort. My second thought is to express some pleasure that it is again possible to debate a measure which is so important and which should be very carefully considered before parliament takes action on the proposal of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue).
In my contribution to the debate, Mr. Speaker-and I hope I will be reasonably short-I should like to present some figures which would suggest that if we adopted this measure the small loans companies of Canada would immediately disappear from the landscape because they would all be forced out of business by bankruptcy. To this I have no particular objection. Fortunately I have never had to use their services but it still is a fact that we should consider that if we were to give effect to this measure it would mean the disappearance of the loan companies.
The reason I say that is that according to figures compiled by one of these companies the costs of operating their services amount to about 13.3 per cent of the average outstanding on loans. The hon. member for Assiniboia proposes that the effective rate of interest should be 12 per cent and it is apparent on the face of it that 12 per cent is less than 13 per cent. I am not going to vouch for the accuracy of these figures. They are but projections and would have to be carefully examined in a committee. Notwithstanding whether or not they are correct, it is still an assertion by one company which has compiled these figures that if the effective rate of interest was set at 12 per cent the loan companies would immediately suffer losses.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
If, as he states, the figure is 13 per cent for the operation of such businesses, can I assume that the hon. member is in favour of operating inefficient businesses?

Mr. Speaker, the question is simple but I am afraid the answer will have to be somewhat complex. The trouble is that the people who have to use the services of small loans companies are the unfortunates of the world and the unfortunates of the world do not always find it easy to obtain the money they need on simple terms. They are the people who go to the

small loans companies or loan sharks, and may I say I have no objection to the use of that term. If the money is to be repaid they are the people who have to be hounded by the collectors who work for the loan companies and by their letter writers, and all this adds up to cost. Unfortunately, it must be paid for out of the business. I certainly am not in favour of this business. Most of the people are honest and do repay the money in time, but still the collection of money from these other people is a very expensive item and it adds to the cost of operation of these companies.
I think that is a point that has to be faced squarely. Assuming that the cost of operation is that high-I would think that would have to be very carefully examined because, as I have said, I am only passing on the information I have received from one of these companies-and assuming these companies did disappear, the inevitable result would be that the people who needed the money and who had gone to these loan companies before would have to find their money from other sources. I would suggest they would find that money, Mr. Speaker, by going to bootleg sources. If a man is desperate, he will pay almost anything to obtain what he wants.
Those are the facts, and they cannot be ignored. This is not the best of all possible worlds. Some of these people are the victims of their own circumstances. They do not enjoy a first class bank rating, for example, so many of them would find difficulty in borrowing money from credit unions. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I am looking at the number of accounts in Canada under the small loans operations for a year and I find there are approximately one million. There are only 213,000 Canadians who have loans of more than $1,100. I am looking at the figures which were compiled for, and set forth in the annual report of the department of insurance for 1958. These are precisely small loans, Mr. Speaker, when people have to borrow up to $1,100.
Would my hon. friend permit a question?
Yes, indeed.
Do those figures to which the hon. member referred include the financing of automobiles?

I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, I know these figures cover the operations of all licensed lenders in Canada and I presume they would include the financing of automobiles. However, I cannot give a categorical answer.
May I suggest, sir, that there are two types of people who go to the small loans companies
Interest Act
for loans at interest rates which go up to 24 per cent. The first group would be those who are misled by the advertising or who are ignorant of the actual rates they are paying and so go to the premises of the loan companies. The second group would be those who are beyond what I call the twilight zone of basic credit. I mean they have not the standing which would enable them to borrow money at from 6 per cent to 12 per cent from the chartered banks or any credit unions or any of the other reputable sources. The remedy, apart from the bill we are considering, could include education for the former, that is to clearly show the effective rates of interest one pays by going to finance companies. The remedy for the latter group who are forced to go to high interest sources for their money is a very difficult problem. I suggest that this bill cannot be the answer. Before I conclude my remarks, perhaps I may be allowed to present my own solution to this social problem which is an extremely important problem.
First, may I make it clear that the remarks made by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton), who referred to money under certain circumstances as being a commodity, are very true. People have to get bread and butter for their living and a roof for themselves and their families. Under special circumstances they may have to also obtain money for the things they need. Money, therefore, is a commodity that has to be sought on a market in which the factors of supply and demand exist. A person's credit rating will determine how much money can be given. The lending of money, under certain circumstances, can be a life raft to a man. Under other circumstances, it can shackle him and drag him down into a river of debt in which he forages for himself forever among the loan sharks. One pretty method they have for dragging in their clientele is the offer of consolidation. We hear that so frequently. Do not be nagged by a dozen creditors, come in and consolidate your debt. Then, of course, you have one big nag instead of a dozen small nags a month. When the consolidation does not quite work out, the interest that is owing and overdue mysteriously becomes part of the principal. The debt is rewritten, and so the story goes and a small debt becomes a very large debt which can hang like a millstone about a person's neck for all his working days.
Recently I had occasion to examine an example of refinancing in my own city. A man had decided to consolidate two debts on which he was paying interest at 6 per cent, amounting to about $2,500. He secured a second mortgage of $5,200 at 8 per cent, but unfortunately there was a bonus provision

Interest Act
so he actually received two thirds of that $5,200 or about $3,500. He was paying a nominal rate of interest of 8 per cent, but the effective rate of interest when all this was done was 16 per cent, and possibly much greater. Obviously instead of two short term worries which were causing great hardship but which would have been solved in a reasonable length of time, this man adopted a long drawn out process in which he is paying less per month but still exchanging a short term debt for a long term debt under very unattractive circumstances indeed. Perhaps this man could never have solved the problem by the traditional methods. Perhaps no bank would have advanced him the money or he could never have remortgaged with the traditional mortgage companies. Perhaps some method of educating him to the use of this money would have served its purpose and saved this man from decades-I am sure it will be decades-of misery.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could mention my own solution to this problem if I am not straying too far from the subject matter under discussion. It seems to me that circumstances differ when people borrow money. What is usury for one man may very well under the circumstances be life saving and the proper thing to do for another. The person who is a victim under one set of circumstances comes out very well indeed under another set of circumstances, even though the amounts borrowed are the same and the terms of the payment are the same. In short, a person who goes into a contract to buy money and to pay a large rate of interest on it may do so knowing full well the risk he is taking, and accepting that risk knowing that it is for his benefit. On the other hand, he may enter into that contract knowing that he is the victim of his own circumstances, that he is helpless, that he must accept almost any terms that are thrown at him.
It seems to me then that the best approach the law could make to help such people would be this. I am convinced that they should be helped; and if all else failed, I would certainly support this bill and hope that it could be given proper study. Then it seems to me that there should be a discretion in the law-an act to deal with usury, to make it an offence-so to contrive it that all circumstances could be brought forward and a judge or a judge and jury could determine in any one particular case whether there was in fact usury and unfair practice against the borrower. This could be done at the instance of the borrower himself so that if he felt aggrieved he would have his remedy. With policing done by the person himself

instead of the more impersonal policing of society which may not work out in this particular bill, I think we would have an answer.

Mr. Speaker, once again I rise in my place to take part in a debate in which I participated some time ago. I cannot help once again congratulating the hon. member who proposed this bill because I feel that his intentions in this regard were good. I am sure that he means no ill by introducing it. At the same time I am not too sure in my own mind that this bill is going to achieve what the hon. member has in mind.
Much as I am concerned with the possible hardship on the people of Canada by having to pay high interest rates I am more concerned with the thought that they must be able to continue to borrow money. No matter how or where he wishes to borrow the money he needs, and no matter in what circumstances he may have to pay it back, the decision in this regard should be that of the borrower. Today we have an alternative.
It is hardly fair to suggest that if a person has been refused a loan by a bank, he should not be able to borrow money at all. The alternative is the small loans companies. It is true that their interest rates are higher than are bank interest rates but I suggest that this is where the risk factor comes into the picture. If interest is the reward for allowing someone else to use your money, some part at least must be the lender's reward for taking the risk that he may lose his money.
On an individual transaction the amount of reward by way of interest will set the limit on the amount of risk a lender will take. The one thing that bothers me in this bill is that the rate of interest will be set at 12 percent. I am afraid that this figure may fall short of the incentive that may be needed in order to induce lenders to lend money to people in certain categories. I refer specifically to an individual case of which I know in the city of Edmonton, that of a man who was refused a normal bank loan. This individual resorted to the higher interest institution. He was able to get his money there at a time when the interest rate was less important than was the fact of being able to borrow the money. Today that man is a successful businessman. I do not think that man would be in the desirable position in which he is today had he not been able to borrow this money, even at an interest rate which was higher, so as to be able to establish himself.
Risk, however, has an over-all effect on the interest rate covering any particular class of borrowing. There are always some losses. These losses in the money lending business

are part of the cost of running that business. They are just as much an expense as are office help, office rent, the cost of light and water or the maintenance of the office itself. As part of the expenses of the business they, must be included in the selling price of the product. Every borrower therefore must pay part of the cost of losses in his class since it is reflected in the price of the commodity he wishes to borrow. This means that interest will go up or down depending on the degree of losses on that particular class of loan.
Like governments and businesses all over the world, the Canadian consumer also depends on cash loans in order to tide him over emergencies or rough spots. This is a form of service which he has come to expect in much the same way as he expects schools for his children, electricity for his home or life insurance for the protection of his family. The Canadian consumer is willing to pay for these advantages in the form of interest and he expects them to be made available to him.
One important point which many people fail to recognize is that the costs of conducting a credit business are dictated by the size of each transaction. As an example, an institution which could profitably make loans of say $12,000 at 6 per cent interest per annum would find it extremely difficult, I am sure, to make sufficient $200 loans in order to take up that $12,000 at 6 per cent. This conclusion follows because it would require 60 times the amount of work. Obviously then the smaller loans must require a higher rate of interest.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) made reference to a banking and commerce committee which sat some time in the past. I was able to obtain some information on the banking and commerce committee which sat in the House of Commons in 1938, and whose report formed the basis for the Small Loans Act. They recognized this cost factor in making smaller loans and expressed this recognition in the following words:
Quite obviously the purchase of a block of 12-year Canadian government bonds requires little expenditure for investigation and none for supervision; investments in 50 farm mortgages for varied periods entail considerable cost both for investigation and supervision; while the investigation of 1,000 applications to effect loans to 500 people for a few months with meticulous supervision becomes expensive business when expressed as a percentage rate of $100 on a monthly basis.
This quotation emphasizes another important cost factor in connection with consumer loans and interest, the cost of investigating the considerable number of applications which do not result in loans being made. This cost is considerable, as the investigation
Interest Act
of applications which do not result in loans is in many cases as expensive as for those applications which do result in loans. The parliamentary committee referred to in the statement I have just made expressed its main objective as follows:
Throughout its inquiry your committee's objective has been to secure the best procurable rate for the borrower.
It is evident from the exhaustive nature of of the 1956 committee's examination that they had the same objective in view. While keeping in mind that the rate should be set as low as possible in the interests of borrowers, the original committee recognized that, for the same reason, it must also be high enough so that lenders would be able to continue to provide this service. This point is emphasized by the experience in certain of the United States. When changes in the laws reduced rates below the level necessary to produce a fair return to the lenders the supply of licensed capital rapidly decreased. The result was a return of high rate, illegal loans in considerable volume.
In the United States, where small loans legislation was first passed in 1917, a great deal of study has been given to the subject of consumer borrowing by legislative committees. In Great Britain, however, the small loans laws and interest laws are considerably different. The law is not as clear-cut as it is in Canada and the United States. If there is a complaint that the rate in a particular loan transaction is too high, and it is not over 4 per cent per month, the onus is on the borrower to show that the rate is unconscionable. If the rate is more than 4 per cent per month the lender must satisfy the court that it is justified.
During the legislative hearings in 1956 in Great Britain an executive of a British loan company told the banking and commerce committee at that time that in practice most consumer loans are made at a rate of approximately 60 to 70 per cent per annum and that, furthermore, there is no restriction as to the kind of security that may be taken by lenders.
I want to say again that I firmly believe the intention of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is nothing but sincere. However, I do hope that he will give some consideration to allowing some body to study the merits of this bill so that there will be some means of determining a right and just form of interest to be set for small loans in the future. On the grounds that I have put forth this evening, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that if the bill should come to a vote I would have to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, just before the supper break I had mentioned that in considering whether this bill should be voted for or against we had to consider whether it would do more harm than good and consideration of that question, I suggest, requires that we look at the present situation.
The purpose of the bill we are considering this evening is to place on interest rates a ceiling of 1 per cent a month or 12 per cent per annum. I suggest that to look at it properly we should have some real idea whether in this country today anyone is forced to pay more than that a month and, in so far as we can, we should determine what are the factors or circumstances that have caused people to pay more than that rate.
Before proceeding I should say it is not my own personal protection I would necessarily be seeking if I were to speak in favour of this bill. I believe it is fairly well known that while hon. members of this house are

not overpaid they happen to have a credit rating unsurpassed in the country so that we can all go into debt at a much lower rate of interest. Not all people in this country are so blessed. Actually some of my friends and relatives and especially many of those who come to me for help in my legal office find themselves stuck with bills that cost them a great deal in excess of normal bank rates, even more than the bank charges me on my overdrafts, I must add.
A proper consideration of what people are paying by way of interest must in my opinion take into account some of the factors which influence interest rates. Since interest rates are determined, on one side at least, by the willingness of people who have money to lend it to others who want it, it is perhaps a good idea to start with some of those considerations which lead people with money to lend into the lending business. What are some of the factors which induce a man to invest his money in a bank, business or loan company rather than into a service station, garage, saw mill or grocery store? Obviously people enter the business of lending money for the same reason they enter any other business. It is an investment. People invest their money to make a profit.
I suggest that a good starting point in considering some of the possible effects of the bill before us is to examine some of the problems confronting those who go into the finance business. Every business has its own financial problems, even the money lending business. Every business must contend with a few fundamental expenses and must undertake some risks and uncertainties. These are some of the basic factors of the matter of going into a business with the idea of making a profit.
I suggest that financial houses of every nature and kind whatsoever face the same business problems that are faced by our local garage men and corner grocers. To do business you must get business. You must attract customers. You must have something to sell. You must convince the public that you are the person with whom to do business. And so, even in the lending business, it is automatic that you will have one overhead expense, the cost of financing your advertising. It may be that your advertising will cost you in direct proportion to the competition in the field, to the type of audience you must reach and to the type of advertising medium that is necessary to reach that audience which is most likely to need to borrow money.
Next, you must figure on the cost of your own money. Most finance people lend other people's money. Because they are so safe, banks are able to obtain money from people

who are interested in saving, the safest possible way in which they can keep their money and earn interest. Banks lend that money. Most people I know are not accustomed to thinking of bank deposits as a source of loans but banks do business with the money which they borrow from investors. Because of their very secure position they are in the happy circumstance of having to pay a very small premium for the use of it. However, there are others who borrow from banks, including finance companies. I suggest we would be most unrealistic if we failed to take into account the legitimate cost to the finance companies of the money they must borrow from the banks.
I suggest also that whether or not they borrow from the banks, if they are financing, entirely depending on their own capital, they must as a cost of their business include the amount of money that that capital could earn in any other business, even at a modest rate of 5 per cent or 6 per cent at which most people can borrow. So that that is an item of cost of at least 5 per cent or 6 per cent as it is for most businesses.
Naturally they require a staff of personnel. They are making loans and therefore they must have bookkeepers and auditors to check their accounts. They must, as all other businesses do in this complex society of ours, have perhaps a little extra staff to keep track of those records, the keeping of which we have of necessity imposed on them over the years, the returns to this and that government department, income tax deductions, unemployment insurance records, and so forth. The cost of overhead in financial institutions, as in all other businesses, is a considerable item which must be paid for by someone.
Since there is not sufficient lending money, and since lending money is a good business only to the extent that you follow sound business practices, it requires good judgment on the part of management in selecting those with whom they will do business. There is, therefore, a good deal of staff work on every application for a loan. It is necessary to know what type of person you are dealing with, to know what security he has, what are the chances of having your money repaid, and perhaps in some instances a case history of the person with whom you are dealing and his record. It may be necessary to check the value of securities and most of those factors which go into determining that perhaps the most important factor of all is the risk you are running in doing your business.
It is in this business of lending money that we really find the risk factor to be all important. It is a straight case of cash being handed to some person. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that just a cursory glance at

the criminal convictions in this country for any short period of time would indicate that it is not really insulting the Canadian people to suggest that there are some dishonest people among us. In fact, the easier it is to steal money the easier it will be to find the hardest working people among our criminal element. Since the easiest thing in the world to steal and to make use of is money, the financial institutions of all kinds are likely to find that attracted to the market are criminals who calculate that the easiest part of the job is where there is no risk of getting rid of the money when you get it.
Therefore, of necessity investigation must amount to a pretty healthy, shall I say, insurance item in this regard. The financial institutions have to be sure first of all in so far as they can that they are dealing with honest men. But this is really only a start. Even if the borrower is honest, such a factor as his general security rating must be taken into account. Does he have a house and furniture? Does he have a steady job? Has he been long in the community? Does he own a car? How much are his debts? What is the worth of all this?
Next is the extent of the loan, the period for which he wishes to borrow the money. If he looks too good in one way, then why has he not gone to an institution which will charge him less for the money? This in itself could appear suspicious enough to warrant further investigation. All of these questions are most pertinent, because, of course, every mistake that the financial institution makes in this regard means a loss, not just of the interest that is charged for advancing the money but on the capital advance itself.
Now, as I said, I am considering some of the cost factors that people in the business of lending money have to take account of and since those who borrow must of necessity pay all the costs that are incidental to running that business and provide a profit to the man himself before he goes into it, we have in those considerations that I have enumerated some very specific items that are brought to bear. Certainly it cannot be expected that a man who has to build his own house and who has paid for practically all of it and who owes on a $10,000 house only $2,000, who has a car that he has paid cash for and a house full of furniture on which he owes nothing, a steady job that he has held for 10 years or 15 years, and a couple of promotions in between, is going to borrow money, taking into consideration the risk factors, at the same price as a recent high school graduate who perhaps may have married too young, taken a job with a new company in a new location, who does not

own his house and has not had time even to acquire furniture free of debt; who does not own a car but merely has loads of responsibilities and nothing to tie them to that location, and in fact nothing that can probably make them move faster than an overbearing load of debt.
I suggest, therefore, that bearing all this in mind we must find this risk factor of such considerable importance that taking into account all the other costs of running this finance business and allowing first your bank interest as a capital cost of running the business we have an awful lot to squeeze in to make the 5 per cent or 6 per cent that stands between that cost of the capital and that return which this bill suggests should be the maximum in any event for any loan.
But I suggest to my colleagues in this house that we have only begun to scratch the surface when we have considered risk only or the cost of running the business. I suggest that the cost is only one item. Risk is another item. There must also be the attractiveness of the business itself if we are going to induce anyone to lend money or come into the money lending business at all. Therefore, I suggest we must consider what competition there is for the money. Certainly we are old enough and have been around long enough to know that the price you pay for anything may be considerably influenced by the supply of that item at hand. If there are too many automobiles on the local car sales lot in a small town where in fact there are only 40 potential customers and 200 cars, we are going to have what would be called a buyers' market, and it is the same story with money.
In certain circumstances at certain times and in certain localities it may very well be that every basic industry is earning very good profit. It may be that the local retailers, the local service businesses, are earning a return on their capital much in excess of the 12 per cent suggested by the bill and that in these localities at these times and under these circumstances there would not be a single person in the money lending business. I suggest that business conditions may never be quite so good that there is no one in the money lending business but certainly we have seen periods when business generally has been so good that for a period of two or three or perhaps more years people have been able to invest in any number of businesses without the degree of risk that we find in the finance business and with a much better assurance of a higher return on their investment.

I suggest that the basic problem today is that we have not given enough consideration to the fact that over the years we have seen built up in this country so many finance companies, so many lending institutions, so many places where one can get money at interest rates so much in excess of 12 per cent per annum. There must be a reason for the growth of these businesses and there must be a reason for interest rates in excess of 12 per cent.
Obviously the demand is there. We happen to have in this country such a high percentage of people who for various reasons must have money that they are willing to pay more than 12 per cent, and I am suggesting that this is where we run into our major difficulty. I say there are various reasons. I have mentioned the example of the young couple just starting out. The young husband must have a few necessities to furnish a home for his young bride and perhaps he is young and foolish as well as desperate enough to pay much more by way of interest. But between that type of case and our solid businessmen we have any number of independent-minded Canadian citizens who have great faith in their own ability, some of whom, like the one mentioned by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Skoreyko) earlier today, happen to have a greater knowledge of the business in which they wish to become engaged and its opportunities than those in the loan business. All the way down the scale, whether it is a matter of pressing needs of the moment or the vision of a man who is going places in business, each one of these people has for his own reasons, for his own needs and desires and to attain his own ends, decided to pay more than 12 per cent.
When I started my few words on this subject I suggested that every law we introduce here must by its very nature be a curtailment to some extent of the freedoms that we all enjoy. Here is my principal fear with regard to this bill, that up to this time and especially in these days of world tension and a feeling of insecurity generally we have seen and are seeing more and more an attitude of looking to the government to do things for us, to take care of us, to make sure that we do not by our own foolishness get into too hot water and of looking to the government to pull us out of the hot water when we do get into it.
I am suggesting that this is not the spirit that we must foster. This is not the spirit that has made our country a rapidly progressing one. This is not the spirit that is needed for democracy itself. I suggest that those who feel most strongly a necessity for us to mollycoddle people to this extent would really,

In rising to speak on the motion for second reading of this bill and the amendment I first of all, along with so many other members who have spoken, offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) for introducing this bill today. Most members of the house, whether or not they have spoken on the bill and whatever side they have taken in the debate, have expressed the opinion that this is a matter that should be examined and, above all, is a matter worthy of the concern of the house at this time. I certainly agree that it deserves this attention, in particular since the problems of consumer financing and the questions that revolve around the matter of interest on consumer loans are growing in complexity every day.
Actually the instalment buying system, or the method we now have of distributing goods by virtue of the instalment contract, is a relatively new thing. Only a few years ago credit in the consumer line was much simpler than it is today. If a man wished to buy goods he bought them, charged them to his account, if he had credit at the retailer's, or if not he arranged at a bank or with a friend for the credit to carry him over until he could repay his loan.
This was relatively simple and the credit limits of the borrower, or the purchaser, were well defined. But today we have a situation where oftentimes the term "purchaser" and the term "borrower" are synonymous. A large percentage of our people today who go to a store to buy goods-cars, appliances, all manner of household goods-plan while they are there to arrange for the financing of these goods. The retailer has become not only a purveyor of goods but also a financier for many people.
From my experience as a lawyer doing business with finance companies and people who had done business with finance companies, acceptance corporations and instalment buying generally, it seems to me that

more and more people are relying upon the retailer to provide their financing for them and to decide whether or not the financing system is satisfactory.
It seems to me that too few people bother any more to read the finance contract that they sign. Too few understand the agreement they are entering into, and very few seem to appreciate the rate of interest that is involved in the transaction. As a matter of fact the situation as regards the finance companies which dispense funds by way of loans, such as Household Finance, is not as bad as some aspects of the general instalment financing that is done by department and retail stores and, I think, by the acceptance corporations.
The consumer loan companies, as they are called, are now regulated by the Small Loans Act and except in the case of loans under $300 there is a limit now of 12 per cent on loans up to $1,500. Over $1,500 there is no limit in law to the interest which can be charged. I sincerely believe the latter is a field which should be studied very carefully. I understand that while loans in this bracket are not as numerous as smaller loans- generally speaking the consumer finance companies are set up to handle and prefer the smaller type of loan-at the same time loans over $1,500 are becoming more common and the interest rates on them are certainly considerable.
It seems to me, however, that a bill of this type is not the whole answer to the problem. I support the amendment that the matter should be referred to the banking and commerce committee, because it certainly is not a simple problem. The first thought of the ordinary man in the street, or in this house, for that matter, in considering a bill like this is that 12 per cent is enough interest for anybody. Indeed, that is my first reaction. I am sure that in most cases interest of 12 per cent is enough for anybody. Indeed, in some cases it is far too much. But on the other hand I think we have to acknowledge that there is a danger that the passage of this bill would act to prevent people who need and want credit in certain high risk fields from getting it when they should have it. Indeed a case can be made out that there is a certain area of lending where an interest rate of 12 per cent is not at all excessive.
Interest rates are generally set, of course, by supply and demand on the market. I remember when I first began to practice law in my home province of Nova Scotia the prime mortgage rate was 4 per cent. Some 12 years later it was almost double that. The difference was not in the value of the security, because if anything I think the

security of properties in my part of the province was greater in recent years than formerly. But the difference was that the supply of money for mortgages was not nearly as great in the latter part of the 1950's as it was in the latter part of the 1940's.
Since money was not in such great supply the mortgage companies had to pay to the investor a higher bond yield so he would make his money available to them. When they added to that the cost of administering loans they were able to say with justice that they needed a much higher interest rate in the late 1950's than they required in the 1940's, when the supply of money outran the demand in most cases. Supply and demand affects interest rates; there is no question about that.
Another thing that affects interest rates, of course, is the risk involved in the loan. Where interest is considered as the reward paid to a lender for the use of his money it is obvious that a man is not going to lend money for the same reward, or price, on a dangerous risk as he would on a good risk. It is also obvious that that is the reason why on most mortgage risks the interest rate is much lower than it is on unsecured loans. All these factors enter into what the interest rate should be and what it is at any particular time.
For that reason, in considering any proposed legislation such as this bill now before us respecting maximum interest rates, we must consider the various types of loans that are made available and how the bill will affect each type of loan. Anyone who would suggest, for example, that the bank rate should be increased from 6 per cent to 12 per cent, or that the banks should be allowed a maximum of 12 per cent would be scoffed out of court. We feel that for business loans 6 per cent is high enough. At the same time many of us will forgive the banks for not entering into the personal loan business in a big way over the years, with a return limited to 6 per cent.
I have mentioned the risk situation and the supply situation. Another very important factor in determining interest rates-as has been said so many times here today-is the cost of administering the type of loan that is made available. Obviously if I borrow $10,000 from a mortgage company or a bank it costs much less for the lender to earn his interest on that money than if I obtained 100 loans of $100 apiece. The same checking has to be done on small loans as on large ones, because no matter what the amount of the loan the lender wants his money returned.

The cost of lending money is much greater in the case of non-business personal loans. The cost of collecting the money is much greater, and of course we do have to give a margin to the man or the company who is in that field for the extra work, trouble and expense to which he goes. However, I feel that there is one particular area of consumer financing where a 12 per cent interest rate would certainly be sufficient, and I refer to the field of the acceptance corporations.
If I go to a car dealer to buy a car on credit the usual situation is that the dealer, after requiring a certain down payment, will ask me to sign a contract to repay the balance owing on the vehicle along with finance charges. I then sign the contract and also a note in which I undertake to pay separate from the contract the amount of money owing on the car plus the finance charges and usually also insurance charges.
If this were a contract between the dealer and me, and the dealer were wondering whether or not he could collect his money there might be some excuse for the high interest rate in view of the risk factor and the cost of administering the loan. But what actually happens is that the car dealer or the retailer of appliances, as the case may be, has in fact nothing to do with the loan. Rather he assigns that contract and the note to the acceptance corporation. Then I must turn up weekly or monthly to make my payments to the acceptance corporation. The rate of interest on these purchase contracts is usually very high. Certainly the rate is high compared with 6 per cent charged by the banks. I cannot help but wonder what justification there is for such high rates in cases of that kind. The acceptance corporation has much more security than the banker ordinarily does on personal loans. And certainly he has twice the security of the consumer finance company which makes an unsecured loan directly to the customer in its office.
The acceptance corporation first of all has a chattel mortgage or rather a conditional sales contract mortgage on the vehicle. Secondly, the acceptance corporation has my signature on the note so that if it must repossess the car and sell it, I can be sued by it for any deficiency on the resale price. In addition to that, since I have signed a note to the dealer as payee which he has endorsed over to the company, the dealer's signature is on the note as an additional endorser. The security of the acceptance corporation is the vehicle itself, my endorsement and the endorsement of the dealer. Certainly the amount of risk in a transaction of this type is small indeed. Indeed, in actual practice if the car is repossessed the acceptance corporation need not even find a market for it. The company

Interest Act
merely returns it to the dealer, who under his contract with them is bound to pay the acceptance corporation the balance owing on the vehicle. The dealer in turn must sell the car to get what money he can and if he is interested in so doing he may sue the initial purchaser of the vehicle for any deficiency.
My argument is that, in the case of the acceptance corporation merely accepting contracts from retailers, they ask very high interest rates in relation to the risk they take and the work they do. Indeed I might go further and say they take so little risk the interest rate paid to them is chiefly payment for their work of administering the loan in place of the retailer. It seems to me this would be a proper case for an inquiry and perhaps for an agreement with the provinces which would allow a national regulatory act to come into being with respect to acceptance corporations and instalment companies.
I also believe that the instalment purchase system used by department stores and retailers generally, since it is becoming so important in our modern merchandising, is a field that would be well worth our searching inquiry. I feel that conditions could be improved by introducing some regulation to the system. It is vital that our free economy should be kept free; and that we should interfere as little as possible in the producing and merchandising sectors of the nation. But on the other hand it seems to me that this is a sphere where we could well exert some control as we have done in the case of bank loans. I think the public and the nation would be better off as a result of some machinery to regulate interest charges on instalment contracts particularly in the field of lending of acceptance corporations.
Certainly, however, the answer to the whole problem of the modern citizen in relation to the retailer-financier is not to be found solely in regulation. Some hon. members have spoken of the work done by the credit unions in providing a source of credit to people who otherwise would be unable to obtain it except at high interest rates. While this work has been important, even more important has been the educational work the credit unions have done in this field. Many people who knew little or nothing about financing or modern merchandising methods before joining a credit union, or coming into contact with credit union philosophy, have achieved a better understanding of modern business and of the type of contracts they were entering into with the retailer on the street and merchandise dealers generally, as a result of credit union educational programs.
[Mr. MacLellan.l
The best answer is education. Before children leave school they should have some knowledge of interest and instalment purchasing. It seems to me there are too few people who really understand how much interest can increase the cost in the purchase of a car, a home or other goods. Few realize how much the cost of goods can be increased by high interest rates. Certainly it is as important to children as any other part of their education that before they leave school they should be taught what instalment contracts involve and the fundamentals of modern buying and selling.
I agree in principle with the mover of this bill and of the amendment. I hope this subject can be studied more exhaustively either by the banking and commerce committee or a special committee because it is a field which will bear more inquiry as years go on and the merchandising methods of today are extended to additional products.
Instalment contracts have gone hand in hand with mass production and probably mass production and the cheap goods resulting therefrom would not have been possible without the combination of modern merchandising and financing. We reach into many fields to see that the public is protected and to ensure that there is little room for fraud, exploitation and the operation of the clip artists. We could well do it in this sphere as well.

No one has challenged the principle of the arguments or the purpose of the bill today. I think all members of this house, if they approach this question fairly, recognize that the bill aims to deal with a financial cancer and evil that exists in our society because of the needs of certain people who find themselves in difficult circumstances.
I want to say that while I think it is essential that we have some legislation along the lines suggested by this Bill No. C-3 as moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia, I do have great faith in the value of the credit unions mentioned by the hon. member for Timmins in assisting, shall I say, or co-operat. ing with legislation in overcoming the grip these financial companies have on those who

are in need of short term credit to alleviate certain difficult and temporary circumstances. I have had some experience in that respect. I like this idea of legislation and rank and file action in the work of the credit unions in finally removing, shall I say, the evils we are seeking to remove. I think both are necessary.
We have been very successful with the credit union movement in Kootenay West. I can never speak on this subject without mentioning my constituency. We have a number of these credit unions in such places as Ross-land, Trail, New Denver and Nakusp. I remember 10 of us got together many years ago to form a credit union with $200. A lot of the hon. gentleman's friends laughed at us on that occasion and said the workingman is not capable of running his own affairs. Fancy running a bank; they will go broke in four years. Now, I cannot remember the figures, but I think the Trail credit union has assets of $4 million, and I know some people have been advised to go to the Trail credit union to get loans that the bank would not provide. This actually happened during the last year. It is training in the practice of the principles of economic and social democracy. I say we want legislation to supplement the activities of these, shall I say, rank and file organizations.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I must say we support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) which proposes that this bill be referred to the banking and commerce committee for consideration and report. Conditions have changed in the last few years. I think this was a sensible amendment. I want to say right here that I consider the hon. member for Welland a very practical and common sense member. He does not speak at great length. I never saw a doctor who could needle a lawyer to better advantage when it comes to financial questions than the hon. member for Welland. I think his suggestion is a good one, and we support it. It is obvious the members on the government side of the house are not going to allow this bill to pass. They are going to talk it out. I have seen the whip running in and out trying to get some of the boys to come along and carry on the debate. I understand how this is done.
We support this amendment because it is obvious the bill is going to be talked out. I believe the hon. member for Vancouver South supported the amendment timidly but, as he suggested, it will provide an opportunity for a committee to study this question, which is a serious question. An opportunity will be provided to hear representations from credit unions, from trade unions, farmers' organizations and other types of organizations, as

well as from the finance companies themselves. We will have an opportunity to get the facts as they are at the present time and make a report to this house.
Surely no one can object to that. No one who has any concern about the welfare of these people and who recognizes the need for legislation of this type can oppose the amendment moved by the hon. member for Welland. This procedure will provide the facts, the opinions and the opportunity for a report to this house. I am certain that report will further strengthen the opinion of the members of this group as to the need for legislation to correct the present situation.
In conclusion I make this request of members on the government side of the house. If I am correct, I presume that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, could use his tremendous influence within the party to which he belongs with a view to having them support this amendment this evening so that this matter could be referred to the banking and commerce committee as recommended by the hon. member for Welland. I may be wrong. It may be the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois)-I note that he is taking a great interest in the question-or it may be the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) or it may be the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Dinsdale). I know that he is a man of heart. He is a man of principle whom I respect as I respect the others. I urge the responsible cabinet minister or the person on the government side this evening responsible for leading the house that he pass the word around to their members that this is a golden opportunity presented to them by the introduction of this bill and by the hon. member for Welland to have this question studied, to have the public concerned present evidence and make representations and to have the banking and commerce committee make a report so that at least next session we shall have legislation to which the government can point with pride as something to the advantage of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, just a few words to express my views on Bill C-3 now before us and which deals with the limitation of interest rates.
The buying power of a country is the criterion of its economic strength. Whether you live in town or in the country, when the goods put up for sale by large or small 90205-6-80

dealers do not sell because there is no money about, it clearly indicates bad times.
It is obviously among the small people that you find an often unfulfilled wish to buy. One man wants clothing or toys for his family; another wants to buy furniture. Others again dream about owning a car.
Anyway, people want to buy, but have they always got the necessary money? It is at this point that the loan companies come in. They advertise everywhere, in the papers, on the air, on television, in short they use all media of publicity.
Now here is the man who has obtained some money thanks to a loan. He is pleased, and buys what he wants. But the finance company which has given him this loan will expect each month a call from that small wage earner. And he will have to pay to the last cent, not only the amount lent to him, but also unduly high interests.
Everybody has a right to live, of course. A finance company cannot operate and survive without guarantees. The man who asks a bank or a credit union for money to pay his mortgage, must give some guarantee for his solvency; this is but normal.
But, if it is used to strangle the borrower, it must be avoided.
The bill now submitted to us is a step in the right direction. It aims at lowering to a maximum of 12 per cent the interest rate on loans.
I feel that it is the duty of any government to administer the affairs of the nation and to protect its citizens. This field offers a good opportunity to give such protection. Any abuse is to be condemned. There should be no usurers in this world of ours.
I am not an expert in the legal field but I know, as a businessman, that this bill has some merit. Many years ago people who could not pay their debts were sent to jail. Society has become more civilized and the law has been wisely modified.
I am one of those who believe that everyone has a right to live. There should be no hardship in this world. Luxury is out of reach for the poor while the destitute lack the necessities of life.
It is understandable that at one time or another one should have to borrow money. One is short of money and goes to a lending institution which grants the loan but this does not give the institution the right to strangle the borrower by charging him prohibitive interest rates.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the principle of this bill is good and deserves my support.

In my constituency, there are many people who live in small towns, others in rural areas on farms. They all have the right to live and be happy. And I am happy to see, when I visit rural areas, that many enjoy television and that many have a car to drive around.
It is a good sign. It means that business is not so bad after all.
However, much remains to be done. Perfection is not of this world. However, I think our government has shown its willingness to help the people of Canada by providing means for better technical training. Let us at the same time protect people from profiteers, it will be a further good answer to our many problems.
